results.claim: Let D(m,n) be the maximum push number of a sortable m×n instance, N=mn, s=min{m,n}, and t=max{m,n}. Then D(m,n)=O(N·min{s,log t}).
results.proof_sketch:
Assume 2≤m≤n. Run FillColumns on the n×m transpose, with transposed target coordinates. Its potential proof extends to every p×q matrix: a column rotates at most p−1 times; with f underfull columns, each q buffer-row rotations decrease the wrong-body potential by at least f/2. In the phase q/2^i≤f<q/2^{i−1}, the potential is below (p−1)q/2^{i−1}, so fewer than 4p full q-rotation blocks occur. Thus FillColumns costs O(pq log q), and FloatMinimums costs O(pq).

For p=n,q=m, body-full transposed columns imply only that every non-buffer token is in its target original row and that the m buffer tokens occupy the original first column; their row order may be wrong, exactly as the audit observes. Apply the completion lemma below, which first repairs this buffer-column permutation and then sorts within rows in O(mN) pushes, including the odd×odd parity case. The resulting bound is O(N log m+mN)=O(mN). Combining it with the source's O(N log n) algorithm gives O(N·min{m,log n}); symmetry gives the claim. One-dimensional boards are sortable, when sortable at all, with O(N) pushes.

results.claim: For every fixed s≥2, boards with min{m,n}=s have asymptotically tight push number D(m,n)=Θ(mn).
results.proof_sketch: The preceding upper bound becomes O(mn) when s is fixed. For the lower bound, translate the sorted board simultaneously by floor(n/2) columns and floor(m/2) rows. The exact-distance calculation below gives m floor(n/2)+n floor(m/2)=Ω(mn). Thus the logarithmic gap is completely closed for every fixed-width family.

results.claim: Every instance A has the displacement certificate pn(A)≥ceil(H(A)/n)+ceil(V(A)/m). Moreover, a global translation by a columns and b rows has exact push number m·d_n(a)+n·d_m(b), where d_k(z)=min(z mod k,k−(z mod k)).
results.proof_sketch:
Let H(A) be the sum, over all tokens, of cyclic horizontal distance from the token's current column to its target column; define V analogously. A row push moves n tokens one horizontal edge, so it changes H by at most n, while column pushes leave H unchanged. Hence at least ceil(H/n) row pushes are necessary. Similarly at least ceil(V/m) column pushes are necessary, and these bounds add.

For a global translation, H=mn·d_n(a) and V=mn·d_m(b), giving the stated lower bound. It is attained by rotating every row d_n(a) times in the shortest reverse direction and every column d_m(b) times likewise. In particular, the half-translation has exact distance m floor(n/2)+n floor(m/2)=mn−[m(n mod 2)+n(m mod 2)]/2.

results.claim: For m,n≥2, a sharper general counting lower bound is D(m,n)≥ceil(log_{d−1}(1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d)), where d=2(m+n), Q=(mn)! if m or n is even, and Q=(mn)!/2 otherwise.
results.proof_sketch: There are Q sortable configurations by the parity characterization. Any shortest word has no adjacent generator-inverse pair. Using the nominal d directed generators, the number of reduced words of length at most L is at most 1+d·((d−1)^L−1)/(d−2). If every sortable configuration were within L pushes, this quantity would be at least Q; rearranging gives the formula. Stirling's estimate yields D≥[N log N−N+O(log N)]/log(2(m+n)−1). In particular, for bounded aspect ratio this is (2−o(1))N. The restriction m,n≥2 is essential: in one dimension some nominal pushes are identities or coincide and the parity characterization does not give Q; for example, a 1×11 board has only 11 sortable cyclic shifts and diameter 5, while the unrestricted old formula returns 6.

results.claim: Global translations are not generally diametral: D(2,3)=7, whereas every translated 2×3 board has distance at most 5.
results.proof_sketch: Exact breadth-first search with the seven distinct unit generators visited all 6!=720 configurations, with level sizes 1,7,31,115,274,253,36,3. Thus the diameter is 7. The configuration with rows (3,2,1) and (6,5,4) is at level 7; a shortest identity-to-configuration word is R1-left, C1, R1-left, C1, C3, R1-right, C1. The exact translation formula gives maximum translation distance 2 floor(3/2)+3 floor(2/2)=5.

results.claim: On an a×b board with a,b≥2, every even permutation of the positions of one specified row can be performed in O(ab) unit pushes while fixing every other position; the analogous statement holds for a specified column. If a or b is even, every permutation of a specified row or column can be performed this way.
results.proof_sketch:
For an even row permutation π, Lemma 10 factors π into involutions σ and υ having the same number k of transpositions. Apply the source's SwapPairs construction to σ and υ with opposite side-effect directions. Lemma 8 is positional and assumes no sortedness: both calls use the same k auxiliary columns, their body shifts cancel, and every position outside the selected row is restored. Since k≤b/2, the cost O(ka+b) is O(ab).

If b is even, one unit rotation of the selected row is an odd b-cycle; pre- or postcomposing an odd π with it leaves an even permutation for the preceding construction. If b is odd and a is even, use π=συτ as in Lemma 10. The σ,υ calls cancel their side effects. The τ call leaves only a cyclic shift of the a−1 nonselected positions of one auxiliary column. Since a−1 is odd, this cycle is even, so its inverse is performed exactly by the even construction on the transpose. This restores every off-row position in O(ab) pushes. Cyclic symmetry permits any selected row, and transposition gives the column statement.

results.claim: Let 2≤m≤n and N=mn. If every token whose target column is not 1 lies in its target row and the m target-column-1 tokens occupy column 1, then every sortable such board can be sorted in O(mN) pushes.
results.proof_sketch:
Let β be the column-1 permutation that puts the buffer tokens into their target rows. If either dimension is even, the line-permutation lemma performs β exactly in O(N), then performs each required row permutation exactly in O(N), for total O(mN).

Suppose both dimensions are odd. Every legal push is even. If β is even, perform it exactly. The product of the subsequent row corrections is then even. Perform each even row correction exactly. For every odd row correction, choose the same adjacent-position transposition P_i and first perform an even factor leaving P_i. Two residual P_i's can be paired: on adjacent rows, two suitably oriented L-shaped 3-cycles compose to the two horizontal transpositions. Each L-cycle is a four-push row-column commutator. Chaining adjacent-row pairs realizes P_rP_s in O(m) pushes. All pairs cost O(m²)≤O(N).

If β is odd, after full buffer correction the row corrections have odd product. Choose an odd row correction π_r and an adjacent vertical transposition P through its column-1 cell. Factor β as an even column permutation followed by P and perform the even factor. Choose an adjacent horizontal transposition T in row r through the same cell. Performing P then T is one L-shaped 3-cycle, hence four pushes. The remaining correction in row r is even; the other odd row corrections now occur in pairs and are handled above. Thus all effects are exact and the total cost is O(mN).

final_writeup:
The audit's 2×3 counterexample is valid against the parent proof: body-full columns after transposition do not imply correct full token sets in the original rows. The missing heads are buffer tokens, and they can remain in the wrong rows. The revision therefore does not retain that implication. It instead adds an explicit buffer-column correction.

Assume 2≤m≤n and transpose the board while transposing its target coordinates. The FillColumns potential analysis remains valid for the resulting n×m matrix even though it has more rows than columns. For a p×q matrix, each column rotates at most p−1 times. If f columns are underfull, every q rotations of the buffer row decrease the wrong-body potential by at least f/2. Dividing values of f into O(log q) dyadic phases bounds each phase by O(pq) pushes. FillColumns therefore costs O(pq log q), and FloatMinimums costs O(pq).

After these procedures with p=n and q=m, every non-buffer token is in its target original row. The m buffer tokens—those targeting the first original column—are all in that column but may be permuted among its rows. This is precisely the state missed in the parent.

The correction uses an exact line-permutation gadget. Any even permutation of one row or column can be realized in O(N) pushes while fixing every other position: factor it into two involutions with equal numbers of transpositions and run the source's SwapPairs construction with opposite body-shift directions. The side effects cancel. If either board dimension is even, an arbitrary odd line permutation is also exact in O(N): either remove its parity with one unit rotation of an even-length line, or use the odd construction underlying Lemma 11 and cancel its even auxiliary-body cycle on the transpose. These are positional statements and do not require the surrounding tokens to be sorted.

Thus, when a dimension is even, first correct the buffer column and then sort each of the m rows, using O(mN) pushes. On an odd×odd board, only even global permutations are possible. An even buffer correction is performed directly; the odd row corrections then occur in pairs. A prescribed adjacent transposition can be factored from each odd row correction. Adjacent rows' two residual transpositions are products of two L-shaped 3-cycles, each realized by a four-push row-column commutator; chaining these gadgets joins nonadjacent rows. Their total cost is O(m²)≤O(N).

If the buffer correction itself is odd, factor it into an even column correction and an adjacent vertical transposition P chosen through a row whose later correction is odd. Combine P with an adjacent horizontal transposition T factored from that row correction. The operation P followed by T is one L-shaped 3-cycle, so four pushes perform both at once. The remaining row correction there is even, and all other odd row corrections pair as above. This completes every sortable intermediate board in O(mN) pushes.

Consequently D(m,n)=O(Ns). Combining this with the source's O(N log t) construction proves D(m,n)=O(N·min{s,log t}). The exact translation lower bound gives D(m,n)=Ω(N), so D(m,n)=Θ(N) for every fixed s≥2.

This is only a partial resolution of the stated target. For balanced and other regimes with s≥log t, the surviving general bounds remain Ω(N) and O(N log t); the logarithmic gap is not closed. The displacement certificate, factorial reduced-word bound, and exact value D(2,3)=7 are retained, but none by itself supplies the missing general lower or upper bound.

The factorial reduced-word bound is asserted only for m,n≥2. On that domain every nominal unit push is nonidentity, the source's parity characterization gives the stated Q, and deleting adjacent inverse pairs gives the reduced-word overcount even when two direction labels coincide on a length-two line. In one dimension these hypotheses fail: for example, a 1×11 board has only 11 sortable cyclic shifts and diameter 5, while the unrestricted old formula returns 6.
